column1: Why does the human eye get drawn to certain elements in a composition before others?
column2: Because visual hierarchy exploits involuntary biological mechanisms (contrast detection, edge recognition, pattern matching) — the eye is drawn to discontinuities like sudden shifts in size, value, or isolated saturated color, which cannot be consciously ignored.

column1: In color theory, which perceptual channel is most critical for visual clarity, and what common novice mistake results from ignoring it?
column2: Value (relative lightness/darkness) is most critical — human vision is acutely sensitive to value contrast. Novices often over-rely on hue variation while neglecting value contrast, producing muddy compositions that lack clear structure.

column1: Why is 12 the de facto standard number of columns in web grid systems?
column2: 12 is highly divisible — it factors cleanly into halves, thirds, quarters, and sixths — allowing a single grid to support 2, 3, 4, or 6-column layouts without separate layout definitions.

column1: What is the core invariant of responsive grid design?
column2: Column count, gutter width, and margin size must adapt to viewport width while preserving proportional relationships between elements — responsive design is architectural transformation at breakpoints, not linear miniaturization.

column1: What three nested containment levels structure spatial reasoning in grid-based design?
column2: 1) Outermost container (page margins, max content width), 2) Grid container (divides space into columns), 3) Grid items (span one or more columns based on content and hierarchy).

column1: What is the action-perception loop in interaction design?
column2: A closed feedback cycle where user action triggers visible system response, which informs the user's next action — when it operates within perceptual thresholds, the interface feels transparent/invisible.

column1: What are the three key perceptual time thresholds for interaction feedback, and what happens at each?
column2: ~100ms = feels instantaneous; ~1 second = maintains flow; ~10 seconds = retains attention. Exceeding these thresholds makes the system feel like an obstacle instead of a transparent extension of thought.

column1: What is an 'affordance' in interface design, and what happens when it is false or hidden?
column2: An affordance is an action possibility an object presents through its visual/physical properties (e.g., a button's raised shadow suggests pressability). False affordances (look interactive but aren't) or hidden affordances (interactive but unmarked) force users into trial-and-error, destroying perceived predictability.

column1: What is the central invariant of a design system, called 'referential integrity'?
column2: Every visual property, spacing interval, type scale step, and interactive state must be defined once and referenced everywhere — e.g., a single design token change (like brand color) must propagate atomically across all component instances, not require manual synchronization.

column1: What is the second core invariant of design systems besides referential integrity?
column2: Composability through constraint — the system limits the design space to a finite, well-tested set of parameterized components/variants rather than offering infinite flexibility.

column1: Why can't a 4-column desktop card layout simply shrink linearly for mobile viewports?
column2: Because responsive design requires reflow (e.g., to 2 columns or a vertical stack), re-scaled text for legibility, and expanded touch targets to meet minimum interaction area requirements — not proportional shrinking.

column1: How does typography function as a 'visual grammar' in hierarchical composition?
column2: Typeface, weight, size, line spacing, and letter spacing encode semantic structure and relative importance, placing headings, subheadings, body text, captions, and labels into distinct perceptual registers via consistent scale ratios and spatial rhythms.
